Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
Being in a situation where someone has power over me

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion
make sure to stay close to exit

Memory.value: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing
I feel isolated and set apart from others
I have to be on guard all the time

issues.explanation: For a combat trauma profile, 'kids crying' is not impossible, but it is a relatively specific trigger that would usually be supported by memory or appraisal content involving civilians/children; here the memory and appraisal items do not provide that link, so this trigger is hard to integrate with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: 'My body has been permanently damaged by what happened' implies an enduring physical injury theme, but the rest of the selected items do not support a bodily injury-focused combat presentation: memory items emphasize fragmentation/unreality, triggers emphasize intrusion/power imbalance, and strategies emphasize avoidance/hypervigilance rather than injury management. This appraisal is insufficiently anchored in the rest of the profile.

vignette: Kalia was twenty-two when the combat in the highlands left the sky open and loud. The deployment lasted fourteen months, marked by relentless rotors that thumped against the humid air and commanders whose shouted orders held the weight of life and death. She remembers the fighting in disconnected pieces-a sudden burst of gunfire, the heavy canvas of her gear, the way dust settled over the perimeter. When she tries to hold it all together, the story feels so extreme she doubts it actually belonged to her. She knows exactly what happened, yet when others ask, she finds the words slipping away, leaving only the weight of what she lived. Now sixty-six, Kalia carries her Oceanian heritage with quiet pride, her American citizenship settled into the steady rhythms of her daily life. In the years that followed, her days accumulated into quiet routines. She learned to keep her distance, moving through the world while remaining set apart from the easy chatter around her. After her divorce, she settled into a modest home, yet she avoided going out when the roads grew busy or the crowds thickened, finding that staying close to her own space required less of her. When emotions rose, she allowed them to pass without fully sinking into them, worried that giving in to any strong emotion would let too much flood through. She always chose seats near the door, her body naturally orienting toward the way out, as though positioning herself for a quick retreat. Her office as a curriculum designer sits on the second floor of a glass-walled administrative building, directly under a flight path. The regular sweep of overhead helicopters draws her attention immediately. Each time the sound deepens and rolls across the windows, an intrusive memory of the highlands arrives unbidden, pulling her back into the sudden, heavy stillness of those combat years. The air traffic does not merely echo; it pulls the past forward without warning. At work, she designs instructional programs for public schools, attending weekly review sessions where superintendents and district directors weigh in on her proposals. A director raising a hand settles power over the room, and Kalia feels the familiar shift. She nods, makes notes, and waits for the moment to slip away. She has come to believe that trusting her own judgment is difficult, that she might choose wrong and not see it until later. Her hypervigilance is a constant companion, a quiet alertness that keeps her muscles ready even when nothing is wrong. She watches the room, listening for shifts in tone, for the unspoken expectations that might require a response. Her isolation is not a choice but a condition; she attends gatherings but remains set apart, her experiences residing in a space that others cannot quite cross. When she feels herself growing too close to the surface, when a strong emotion threatens to pull at her chest, she steps back, letting the feeling remain where it is rather than letting it move through her. She avoids the open roads and crowded centers, preferring the predictable edges of her neighborhood, where the exits are clear and the routines hold steady. Her PCL-5 score rests at 49, a quiet reflection of the sustained vigilance she carries. What finally brought Kalia to seek help was a morning meeting where the overhead helicopters coincided with a director's decisive gesture, and for the first time in years, she felt entirely alone in the room. She realized that she had spent a lifetime bracing for the wrong decision, staying near the door, keeping her words close, and watching the sky. She came to the clinic hoping to find a way to let the past remain where it belongs, and to trust that she could sit in the room without always being ready to leave.
